name: How land use plan shares are computed
group: Land use plan: classes and methods
plain: Land shares divide plan area by plan area. Place shares divide listings by listings. Water and roads are left out of the land shares but stay in the denominator of the place shares. This entry gives the steps.
definition: Area shares (urban_pct, urbanizable_pct, rustic_common_pct, protected_land_pct and landuse_km2): for each municipality the build sums the area of its plan polygons by group and leaves out water and road. Each share is the group's area divided by the summed area of the four groups, times 100, rounded to one decimal. Place shares (places_on_protected_land, places_on_protected_land_pct, places_urban_pct): each listing is tested against the plan polygons; the share is the listings in the group divided by the listings inside any polygon, including water and road.

coverage.frequency: Fixed to the 2015 plan; recomputed only if the plan or the municipal list changes.

method: landuse.py reads the plan polygons from the Junta de Planificación's official shapefile (reprojected to WGS84) or from the plan's hosted ArcGIS Online copy. Area is the plan's Shape_Area (square meters in the plan's projected coordinates) divided by 1,000,000. A polygon belongs to the municipality named in its Municipio attribute, matched to the 78 names ignoring accents and capitals. A listing belongs to the first polygon that contains its point. The statistics use the full polygons; landuse.geojson is a simplified display copy.
source_detail: Junta de Planificación, Plan de Uso de Terrenos (PUT 2015) (attributes CLASIPUT, Municipio and Shape_Area); Overture Maps places (release 2026-09-23.1, downloaded 1 October 2026); landuse.py build_landuse(); municipality boundaries from Census TIGERweb Generalized_ACS2023 State_County layer 11 (500k, shoreline-clipped)
how_to_read: Use area shares to describe the land and place shares to describe where listed places stand. The two can differ a lot: land that is mostly protected can hold few listings. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 32,369 of the island's 32,541 listings fall inside a plan polygon.
caveats: The area is the plan's polygon area, not the Census land area, so in the 2015 plan a municipality's classified area can be well under its land area (Mayagüez 67%, because the plan has no polygon on Isla de Mona).
A plan polygon whose municipality name matches none of the 78 names is skipped. The plan has one such polygon, a water polygon named Guayanabo, so it changes no share.
The observatory does not include the Calificación (zoning districts) layer of the Junta de Planificación, which was not available when the 2026-10 snapshot was built.

name: Tourism places within a 400 m walk of a stop with a current timetable (%)
plain: Out of every 100 tourism places in the municipality, how many are within a 400 m walk, along mapped roads, of a stop whose published timetable has not ended. It measures places, not residents.
definition: The number of tourism places in the municipality whose walking distance to the nearest stop with a current timetable (tw_m in place_access.json) is 400 m or less, divided by the tourism places counted (access_n), times 100, rounded to one decimal. It is acc_cur400_pct with the distance walked along mapped roads instead of a straight line. The stop can be in another municipality.

coverage.frequency: Recomputed at each full build and at each run of the nightly transit refresh (access.py); the files are rewritten only when a value changes. In the 2026-10 snapshot the access is as of 2026-10-06 (see access_as_of).

method: access.py counts the places with tw_m of 400 or less in each municipality and divides by the counted places. See place_access.tw_m for how the walk is measured.

how_to_read: A high value means most of the municipality's visitor places are a short walk from a stop that has a timetable in force. Compare it with acc_cur400_pct: the gap is the places that are close in a straight line but not on foot. In the 2026-10 snapshot the value is 28.0% island-wide (6,787 of 24,209 places), against 32.2% in a straight line, and ranges from 0.0 to 84.1 (San Juan). 48 of the 78 municipalities have 0.0 and 12 have 50% or more. Most municipalities change little (median 0.0 points), but some drop a lot: Carolina 88.5 to 70.7, Canóvanas by 16.1 points, Vega Baja by 11.9. The Municipality tab shows a live share of the places that pass your filters, not this stored field.
caveats: Along mapped roads, not every way a person can walk. The road file has no footways, paths, steps, pedestrian streets, sidewalks or crossings, and it does not know fences, gates or a road that is unsafe to cross. The visitor-access study (docs/analysis/visitor-access-2026-10) repeated the run on a full OpenStreetMap walking network: the island share within 400 m moved from 26.6% to 27.0%, and municipal shares moved a median 0.0 points (90th percentile 0.99, largest 11.3 in Hormigueros).

1,210 places (1,074 on the default basis, 4.4%) have no walkable road within 150 m and keep their straight-line distance (see place_access.tw_straight). For them the value is a lower bound: the real walk is at least that long.
A stop with a current timetable is not proof of service. A timetable is a schedule: it does not show that vehicles run on time or at all. The observatory has no real-time data.
Públicos (shared taxis and vans), taxis, ride-hailing, rental cars and tour shuttles are in no timetable, so they are not counted.
The values change on the day a feed ends. In the 2026-10 snapshot 9 of the 18 current feeds end between 2026-10-31 and 2027-01-31, among them San Juan's municipal feed (see methods.access_profile).
A municipality with few places can swing widely: the smallest has 36 places, so one place is 2.8 points. Check access_n before you compare shares.

A municipality with no stop counted inside its border (14 in the 2026-10 snapshot) holds the stored value, which is not a measured 0%. The 2D map leaves it unshaded and unranked, and the downloaded municipality table leaves it blank.

name: Residents within a 400 m walk of a scheduled stop (count)
plain: How many residents of the municipality live within a 400 m (quarter mile) walk, along mapped roads, of a scheduled transit stop. It uses 2020 Census counts. It is an estimate: the road map has no footpaths.
definition: Number of residents (2020 Census) who live in a Census block whose internal point is a walk of 400 m or less, along mapped roads, from the nearest scheduled stop (rounded up to whole meters). Scheduled stops are the boarding points in the timetable feeds of ATI and the municipal systems, including feeds whose timetable has expired. It is pop_served_400m measured by walking instead of a straight line. The stop may lie in another municipality.

coverage.frequency: Recomputed in each full build and by the nightly transit refresh when a feed changes, from the road file the site publishes (roads.bin).

method: network.py (coverage) joins each of the 36,570 populated 2020 Census blocks, at its internal point, to the nearest walkable road within 150 m, and searches the walking network of walknet.py (every road of roads.bin except motorways and motorway links, both directions) from every scheduled stop up to 1,000 m. The walk is the connector, the path along the roads and the stop's connector, rounded up to whole meters, and never shorter than the straight line. A block with no walkable road within 150 m keeps its straight-line test: 4,002 of the 36,570 blocks, with 455,383 residents (13.9%), in the 2026-10 snapshot. A stop with no walkable road nearby counts at its straight-line distance.
source_detail: 2020 Census block population and internal points (TIGERweb Census2020 layer 10); ATI (Autoridad de Transporte Integrado) and municipal GTFS (General Transit Feed Specification) stops; roads from OpenStreetMap (site/data/roads.bin, ODbL)
how_to_read: It estimates how many people live a short walk from a stop. It does not say whether a bus comes, how often, or where it goes. In the transit data of the 2026-10 snapshot, 510,146 of the island's 3,285,874 residents (15.5%) live within a 400 m walk of a scheduled stop, against 925,788 (28.2%) in a straight line. Stops along main roads, and housing that reaches them only through an entrance or around a block, explain most of the gap.
caveats: Along mapped roads, not every way a person can walk. The road file has no footways, paths, steps, sidewalks or crossings. On 2026-10-16 the same count on the full OpenStreetMap walking network (footways, paths and service roads included) gave 15.5% of residents within 400 m of a scheduled stop, against 15.6% on roads.bin, and municipal shares moved a median 0.0 points (largest 1.7, Carolina).

Each block joins the network at the road nearest its internal point. A large block (a housing complex, a condominium) that fronts an avenue on one side but lies nearer a back street reads a longer walk than its residents may make. Joining each block also to every road within 60 m raises the island share from 15.5% to 17.1% (within 100 m: 19.1%), still far below the straight line (28.2%). Read the share as a careful estimate, with about that range around it.

13.9% of residents (455,383, in 4,002 blocks) live in blocks with no walkable road within 150 m of their internal point. They keep the straight-line test, which can only count them nearer than they are, so for them the walking share is an upper bound.
Stops of expired timetables count. For stops with a timetable still running, see pop_walk_active_pct.
Every resident of a block is placed at the block's internal point. Residents are 2020 Census counts, and the stops are those of the current transit data.

name: Land in each class of the land use plan (km², by municipality and for Puerto Rico)
plain: How many square kilometers of each municipality, and of all of Puerto Rico, the 2015 land use plan puts in each of its classes: urban, land for planned or reserve growth, ordinary rural, and the kinds of specially protected rural land. It is the data behind the land-use analysis.
definition: landuse_summary.json holds one field per class (SU, SURP, SURNP, SRC, SREP, SREP-E, SREP-A, SREP-H, SREP-EH, SREP-AH, AGUA, VIAL): the km² of that class in each municipio (municipios, keyed by name, listed in names), in Puerto Rico (puerto_rico, the sum of the municipios) and in polygons with no municipio (unassigned). classes gives each class its label, group (urban, urbanizable, rustic, protected, water, road), color (the map's) and in_share: false for water (AGUA) and road rights-of-way (VIAL), which shares of land leave out. SREP covers the specially protected rural land with no sub-class of its own color (codes such as SREP-AE, SREP-EP, SREP-EA, SREP-P, SREP-AP), as the map draws it.

coverage.frequency: Fixed to the 2015 plan; recomputed only if the plan or the municipal list changes.

method: landuse.py (class_summary) adds the Shape_Area of the full-resolution polygons (square meters in the projected CRS, divided by 1,000,000), by class and by municipio, before the display copy is simplified. Rounded to 0.001 km². The four groups add up to the landuse_km2 of municipalities.json, which the urban_pct, protected_land_pct and the other share fields divide by.
source_detail: Junta de Planificación, Plan de Uso de Terrenos (PUT 2015), version of 30 November 2015; attributes CLASIPUT (class), Municipio and Shape_Area
how_to_read: Divide a class by the land in the plan (all classes with in_share) for a share; the analysis does it for you. In the 2026-10 snapshot Puerto Rico has 8,409.1 km² of land in the plan: 14.2% urban, 0.8% for urban growth, 21.3% ordinary rural and 63.7% specially protected rural, most of it agricultural (27.7%) or ecological (21.3%). Cataño is 99.9% urban and San Juan 79.6%; Maricao is 96.7% specially protected and Las Marías 94.3%.
caveats: A planning classification, not land cover: it says what the plan allows or protects, not what is on the ground today. Land marked urban can be undeveloped, and protected land can hold homes.
A single plan, adopted on 30 November 2015. Amendments and municipal plans adopted since are not included.
Areas are planar, from the plan's projected coordinates; they can differ slightly from other area figures (land_km2) that come from Census boundaries.
